accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE 2013 Key Stage 3 science programme of study (physics: 'the density of materials'; particle model of solids, liquids and gases) and AQA GCSE Physics 8463 section 4.3.1.1 (ρ = m/V, units kg/m³, required practical on regular and irregular solids by displacement). Densities were checked in the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics and Kaye & Laby tables: cork 0.24, pine ~0.5, candle wax ~0.9, ice 0.917, olive oil 0.91–0.92, water 1.00, PVC ~1.4, aluminium 2.70, steel 7.85, brass ~8.5, copper 8.96, lead 11.34, steam ~0.0006 g/cm³ at 100 °C and 1 atm. Every lab number was recomputed: 27 g/10 cm³ = 2.7, 54/20 = 2.7, 39.5/5 = 7.9, 12/24 = 0.5, 180/20 = 9.0, 72/8 = 9.0, 50/20 = 2.5, 34/4 = 8.5, 14/10 = 1.4; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

misconceptions.evidence: The documented KS3 density misconceptions are each targeted: heavy means dense / big things sink (step 1 prediction 'the plank, it is heavier' and step 5 prediction 'the pebble, it is lighter'), multiplying or inverting the formula (step 2 distractors m × V and V ÷ m with their own feedback), adding sides or using one face for volume (step 3 distractors l + w + h and l × w), taking the new cylinder reading as the volume (step 4 prediction '70 cm³' and distractors), density changing when a piece is cut (challenge 'half'), and confusing g/cm³ with kg/m³ (challenge 'unit').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdens is built on density's own mechanism: dragging equal 10 cm³ cubes of four metals and wood onto a scale with a live readout, dropping the m ÷ V answer into a ρ box, a drawn cuboid with labelled edges whose volume must be chosen before its material is identified, a measuring cylinder whose water level rises when an object is dragged in, a float/sink tank split at water's 1.0 g/cm³, and particle boxes drawn by spacing and particle size to rank. No other flagship lab uses a balance, a displacement cylinder or density values; lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab, including the particle labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the idea before it is stated: equal cubes give 5, 27, 79 and 90 g, so the same volume clearly holds different mass; the cuboid step only reveals the material after the right volume, so the child sees density identify a substance; the cylinder visibly rises from 50 to 70 and the options force a choice between the reading and the difference; the tank files a 0.24 g/cm³ cork at the top whatever its size; and the particle boxes show lead and aluminium with the same packing but heavier particles.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each hold a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'the plank, it is heavier' (equal cubes show pine at 0.5 vs steel at 7.9 g/cm³), '70 cm³' for the pebble (the cylinder step accepts only 70 − 50 = 20 cm³) and 'the pebble, it is lighter' floats (the tank floats every object under 1.0 g/cm³ regardless of size). The completion line names the learner's own pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; every wrong option has its own tag and message: 'times' (that multiplied, divide), 'flip' (volume ÷ mass, mass goes on top), 'reading' (55 is water plus toy), 'add' (subtract the readings), 'sum' (adding sides gives a length), 'face' (3 × 2 is one face), 'size' (amount does not matter, 0.92 < 1.0), 'mix' (the less dense liquid sits on top), 'half' (mass and volume both halve) and 'unit' (a m³ holds a million cm³).

readability.evidence: Measured with learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 4.4 (family limit 5.0) and adult 6.4 (limit 10.0). Kid paragraphs give one idea each with a worked case (a steel nut and a steel beam are both about 7.9 g/cm³); the terms intensive property and AQA references appear only in the adult text. Lab step headers were shortened ('Odd shapes', 'Regular blocks') so they stay on one line at 360 px.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence gives the formula, a unit, a method or an example; the adult text gives the KS3 and GCSE requirements, why g/cm³ is used, the intensive-property point with table values, named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases, and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson, including Floating and sinking and Mass changes in open and closed systems (769).

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all seven steps: the scale readout first overlapped the cube labels and was moved up (pan at 32% height, short stand), the particle labels first overflowed and were shortened to lead / aluminium / water / steam; after the fixes the four 48 px cubes, the three 52 px answer tiles, the cuboid with edge labels, the cylinder with a 0–100 scale and 'start 50' label, and the full-width tank all fit without clipping. The browser walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button below in the same order as on screen: 'Weigh pine' … 'Weigh copper', the three density answers, the three volumes read as cubic centimetres, 'Drop the pebble in' then the three volume options, floats / sinks with the object named, and the four particle boxes as 'Rank next: …'. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the numbers spoken in words, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.
